physical_harm: Severe injuries including fractured legs and internal injuries leading to death
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the circumstantial evidence, including the 'last seen' theory, forensic and medical evidence, and the identification of the accused by PW-4 and PW-7.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses, including PW-4 (brother of the deceased) and PW-7, as reliable and their statements were considered along with forensic and medical evidence.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 03.02.2013; Trial judgment: 25.06.2013; High Court decision: 25.06.2013; Supreme Court decision: 18.01.2019
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Sanjay R. Hegde, Pranjal Kishore, Dr. Sanjay Gupta, Yash S. Vijay, Dr. Sushil Balwada; Counsel for the State: Ms. Swarupama Chaturvedi, B. N. Dubey, Mukesh Kumar
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted and sentenced; High Court: Confirmed conviction and sentence; Supreme Court: Modified death sentence to life imprisonment with actual period of 25 years
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant, aged about 50 years, took away the deceased from the 'Mela' and committed rape and murder. The evidence included the testimony of PW-4, the brother of the deceased, who identified the accused in the Test Identification Parade and stated that the appellant took away the deceased. PW-1 reported seeing a dog with a child's leg, and the headless body of the deceased was found in the bushes. The prosecution also highlighted the forensic and medical evidence, including severe injuries on the private parts of the deceased and the recovery of blood-stained clothes from the appellant's house.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, as the case rested solely on circumstantial evidence. The appellant claimed he was denied proper legal assistance and is a manhole worker. The defence also submitted that the trial court and High Court did not consider relevant mitigating circumstances and that the death sentence was imposed without examining special reasons under Section 354(3) of the Cr.P.C. The appellant also pointed out that the local Bar Association refused to represent him, leading to inadequate legal representation.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the 'last seen' theory and the test of the 'rarest of rare' cases, emphasizing the need to consider mitigating circumstances and the legislative policy under Sections 235(2) and 354(3) of the Cr.P.C. The Court also referred to the ratio laid down in Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab and other precedents to determine the appropriateness of the death sentence.
precedent_relied_upon: Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 684; Swamy Shradhananda(2) v. State of Karnataka (2008) 13 SCC 767; Neel Kumar v. State of Haryana (2012) 5 SCC 766; Selvam v. State (2014) 12 SCC 274; Tattu Lodhi v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2016) 9 SCC 675; Raj Kumar v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2014) 5 SCC 353; Anil v. State of Maharashtra (2014) 4 SCC 69; Mukesh & Anr. v. State (NCT of Delhi) & Ors. (2017) 6 SCC 1
sentencing_rationale: The death sentence was modified to life imprisonment with an actual period of 25 years, without any benefit of remission, as the case did not fall within the 'rarest of rare' category. The Court found that the reasons assigned by the trial court and High Court did not constitute special reasons under Section 354(3) of the Cr.P.C. to impose the death penalty.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The Court considered the appellant's age (about 50 years), his occupation as a manhole worker, and the lack of finding that there was no possibility of reformation. The Court also noted that the appellant was not adequately represented by legal counsel during the trial.
other_sentence_order: Sentences imposed for all offences to run concurrently. The appellant is to serve life imprisonment with an actual period of 25 years, without any benefit of remission.
